text_blocks.snippet: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is typically managed through a combination of heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when necessary, prescription medications.
snippet_highlighted_words: heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when necessary, prescription medications

text_blocks.snippet: Adopting healthy habits is the first step in lowering blood pressure and can sometimes reduce the need for or amount of medication:

list.snippet: Dietary Approaches (DASH): Follow the DASH Eating Plan, which emphasizes vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on sodium (salt).
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking, swimming, or cycling.
Weight Management: Lose excess weight if you are overweight or obese to reduce strain on your heart and blood vessels.
Limit Alcohol and Quit Smoking: Reduce alcohol consumption and stop smoking or using tobacco, which immediately constricts blood vessels and raises heart rate.
Stress and Sleep: Practice stress-reduction techniques and aim for at least 7 hours of quality sleep per night.

text_blocks.snippet: When lifestyle modifications alone do not lower blood pressure sufficiently—or if you have a high 10-year risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or chronic kidney disease—doctors typically prescribe one or more classes of blood pressure drugs:

list.snippet: Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) Inhibitors: Relax blood vessels to keep them from narrowing (e.g., lisinopril, benazepril).
Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Block the action of chemicals that tighten blood vessels (e.g., losartan, valsartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells, allowing vessels to relax (e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem).
Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help your body get rid of excess sodium and water, reducing fluid volume in the blood; thiazide diuretics are most common (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide).

Single vs. Multi-Drug Therapy: Stage 1 hypertension is often managed with a single medication, while Stage 2 hypertension or higher risk profiles frequently require two or more medications combined—sometimes in a single pill for convenience.
Target Goals: For most adults, the general treatment goal is a blood pressure reading of less than 130/80 mm Hg.

Resistant Hypertension: If blood pressure remains high despite taking three or more medications (including a diuretic), a healthcare provider will investigate underlying causes and adjust the regimen or consider specialized interventions.

text_blocks.snippet: Review official resources from the American Heart Association or the CDC High Blood Pressure Guide for detailed insights on managing your care plan.
